Data centering (xi​↦xi​−xˉ)

Words: 17
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
Data centering subtracts the sample mean from every observation, separately for each coordinate of multivariate data. The resulting coordinate sample means are zero.

Regression analysis

Words: 30
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
Regression analysis studies how a response variable depends on explanatory variables through a regression model. It estimates that dependence and assesses uncertainty in fitted regression coefficients, predictions and model comparisons. Linear regression is one important case.

Mark and recapture

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
Mark and recapture estimates the cardinality of a finite set of individuals when counting everybody is impractical. The useful information is the overlap between observations: with fixed sample sizes, finding many of the same individuals again suggests a smaller population, while finding few suggests a larger one. More elaborate capture-recapture models also estimate survival and changing probabilities of detection.
In a closed-population capture-recapture model, let N be the unknown population cardinality. Capture M distinct individuals, mark them, release them all, and allow them to mix with the rest. Next take a second sample of C distinct individuals using sampling without replacement, and count the R individuals carrying a mark. The observed marked fraction R/C estimates the population's marked fraction M/N, giving the Lincoln-Petersen estimator
CR​≈NM​,NLP​=RMC​(R>0).
(1)
Release happens between the two samples; sampling without replacement means that an individual is counted at most once within the second sample. See Richard J. Barker, Open Population Mark-Recapture Models, §1.1.1.
For a constructed teaching example, mark M=20 individuals and later capture C=25, including R=5 marked individuals. One fifth of the second sample is marked, suggesting that the twenty marked individuals are one fifth of the population:
NLP​=520⋅25​=100.
(2)
Let A and B be the sets of individuals in the first and second samples. Their intersection has cardinality five. By the inclusion-exclusion principle, the set union contains
∣A∪B∣=∣A∣+∣B∣−∣A∩B∣=20+25−5=40.
(3)
Thus N≥40 is an observed lower bound, whereas 100 is the output of an estimator based on the capture-recapture model. These are toy counts, not measurements from a medical or ecological study.
The diagram shows only observed individuals. It does not draw an assumed population of one hundred. The capture-recapture model uses the overlap to infer how many individuals may have escaped both samples; its likelihood function shows why one estimator output cannot describe all that uncertainty.

Capture-recapture model

Words: 838 Articles: 4
Mark and recapture OurBigBook.com
A capture-recapture model is a statistical model for repeated observations of identifiable individuals, including those missed on some occasions. A closed-population capture-recapture model estimates a fixed population cardinality; models allowing individuals to enter or leave can instead describe survival and recruitment. The sampling assumptions determine which likelihood function is appropriate.
For the two-sample closed-population capture-recapture model, condition on the sample sizes M and C. If the second sample selects C distinct individuals from N by simple random sampling, then the overlap R has the hypergeometric distribution:
P(R=r∣N,M,C)=(CN​)(rM​)(C−rN−M​)​,max(0,M+C−N)≤r≤min(M,C).
(4)
Here r is an integer and the probability mass function is zero outside these bounds. The binomial coefficients count choices of r marked and C−r unmarked individuals, divided by all equally likely size-C subsets. The hypergeometric distribution has expected value
E[R∣N,M,C]=NMC​.
(5)
Equating the observed overlap with this expected value gives the Lincoln-Petersen estimator. The underlying sampling without replacement, probability mass function, and expected value are developed in Raymond P. Guiteras, MIT 14.30 hypergeometric distribution handout, §§1–4 and 8.
For the toy counts M=20, C=25, and R=5, hold the observations fixed and vary the unknown integer N. The likelihood function is
L(N)=(25N​)(520​)(20N−20​)​,N=40,41,42,….
(6)
Values below forty cannot contain the observed set union. Exact comparison of consecutive likelihoods gives two tied maximum-likelihood estimates, N=99 and N=100. The Lincoln-Petersen estimator returns 100; the Chapman estimator returns 90 and is a different rule for estimation.
The vertical scale is L(N)/maxn≥40​L(n). This relative likelihood compares how well candidate statistical parameters explain the same observations; it is not a posterior probability. The displayed range 40≤N≤300 is only a plotting window. The likelihood function remains positive for every integer N≥40 and tends to zero as N increases, so the curve has a continuing right tail. The data do not justify truncating statistical inference at three hundred. The conditional hypergeometric distribution formulation also appears in Louis-Paul Rivest and Mamadou Yauck, Small Sample Estimators for Two-way Capture Recapture Experiments, §3, equation (5).
Zero recaptures require care. With R=0 and positive M,C, the Lincoln-Petersen estimator has no finite ratio, but the capture-recapture model still gives a valid likelihood function:
L0​(N)=(CN​)(CN−M​)​,N≥M+C.
(7)
This likelihood function increases toward one as N grows, so there is no finite maximum-likelihood estimate. For the same sample sizes twenty and twenty-five with zero overlap, forty-five distinct individuals would be observed. Lack of overlap supplies a lower bound but very weak information about large population cardinalities.
In more elaborate capture-recapture models, a first-recapture array mij​ counts individuals released at occasion i and next observed at j. A probability of survival ϕj​ and a probability of detection Pj+1​ contribute a no-observation continuation factor ϕj​(1−Pj+1​). The resulting likelihood function depends on both survival and detection; these probabilities need not be separately identifiable at the last observation interval. Missing-count EM for capture-recapture describes one way to fit such a model, and identifiability remains a separate issue from computing an estimator output.

Closed-population capture-recapture model (N=constant)

Words: 308 Articles: 2
Capture-recapture model OurBigBook.com
A closed-population capture-recapture model assumes the same individuals remain throughout the observations: no births, deaths, immigration, or emigration. Its elementary two-sample version additionally requires retained, correctly recognized marks and a second sample chosen by simple random sampling independently of first-sample membership. Mixing and unchanged capture behavior help make this plausible. Equal individual capture probabilities alone do not guarantee that every size-C subset is equally likely; that stronger sampling assumption gives the hypergeometric distribution. See Barker, §§1.1.1 and 1.1.3: closure, marks, and catchability assumptions.
Unequal catchability, mark loss, and population change can invalidate this capture-recapture model. For example, if especially catchable individuals appear repeatedly, overlap can be inflated and the Lincoln-Petersen estimator can underestimate population cardinality. Lost marks can decrease recorded overlap and increase the same ratio estimator, all else equal. Two samples alone cannot establish that the sampling assumptions hold.
Lincoln-Petersen estimator (NLP​=MC/R)
Words: 88
Closed-population capture-recapture model OurBigBook.com
The Lincoln-Petersen estimator is the ratio estimator obtained by matching the observed overlap to its hypergeometric expected value. It is defined when R>0. To distinguish that ratio from the exact integer maximization, consecutive positive likelihoods satisfy
L(N)L(N+1)​=(N+1)(N+1−M−C+R)(N+1−M)(N+1−C)​.
(8)
This comparison is valid for N≥M+C−R. For the toy counts, the numerator minus the denominator is 500−5(N+1). Thus the likelihood function increases up to ninety-nine, ties at ninety-nine and one hundred, then decreases for every larger integer. This independently establishes the global maximum-likelihood estimates, beyond the plotting window. The adjacent-ratio method is given in Guiteras, §8.
Chapman estimator (NCh​=R+1(M+1)(C+1)​−1)
Words: 91
Closed-population capture-recapture model OurBigBook.com
The Chapman estimator is a correction intended to reduce the small-sample bias of the Lincoln-Petersen estimator. Under the fixed-size hypergeometric sampling assumptions it is exactly an unbiased estimator when M+C≥N; it can have nonzero bias otherwise. This qualification and the formula are stated in Barker, §1.1.1, equation (1.3), citing Chapman's work through Seber. For the toy observations,
NCh​=5+1(20+1)(25+1)​−1=6546​−1=90.
(9)
It is an alternative estimator, not a maximum-likelihood estimate for this capture-recapture model. The Chapman estimator remains finite when R=0, but a finite output does not supply the missing overlap information or repair unequal catchability, lost marks, or population change.

Missing-count EM for capture-recapture (E[nij​∣m,ϕ,P]=Ni​wij​/Ci​)

Words: 81
Capture-recapture model OurBigBook.com
Let Ni​=Ri​−∑s=i+1J​mis​ count individuals never recaptured after release i. Partition them into death-interval counts nij​ and terminal survivors niJ​. Their unnormalized weights are wij​=(1−ϕj​)∏ℓ=ij−1​ϕℓ​(1−Pℓ+1​) for j<J, and wiJ​=∏ℓ=iJ−1​ϕℓ​(1−Pℓ+1​). Conditional counts are multinomial with normalizer Ci​=∑j=iJ​wij​. The EM algorithm replaces all missing counts by the displayed conditional expectations, then maximizes the resulting complete-data log likelihood. Survival and detection updates are expected successes divided by expected opportunities. A flat observed-likelihood ridge remains nonidentifiable even if each conditional complete-data maximization is explicit.

Nonlinear regression

Words: 42
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
Nonlinear regression fits a conditional mean whose dependence on its parameters is nonlinear. In a normal distribution observation model, the likelihood is based on residuals yi​−m(xi​,θ). Nonlinearity can create parameter trade-offs, asymmetric uncertainty and several posterior regions, so prior predictive checks and Markov chain Monte Carlo convergence diagnostics can be especially useful.

Outlier

Words: 44
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
An outlier is an observation unusually far from the behavior expected under a statistical model. A large regression residual can identify a candidate, but data validation, regression leverage, and the possibility of model misspecification should be examined before excluding it. An outlier need not be an influential observation.

Regression to the mean

Words: 61
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
An unusually extreme noisy observation tends to be followed by a less extreme observation even without intervention. Selecting locations for an intervention because they had high prior event counts can therefore bias a simple before-and-after comparison toward an apparent reduction. The effect follows from conditioning on an extreme value with a transient random component, rather than from a causal treatment effect.

Response variable (Y)

Words: 48
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
A response variable is the outcome whose variation is described by a statistical model or whose change is compared across treatments. Its unit, measurement procedure and observation time must be specified. An outcome consisting of a feature count is one response per sketch, not one independent experimental response per feature.

Scientific control

Words: 49
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
A scientific control supplies a comparison or procedure that distinguishes an intended effect from other influences on an experiment or observational measurement. Negative controls should show no target effect; positive controls should show a known effect. A negative control outcome applies this logic to an outcome that the exposure cannot causally affect.

Design of experiments

Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com

Fractional polynomial

Words: 50
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
A fractional polynomial uses selected real powers of a positive covariate to model a smooth regression effect. Power zero denotes a logarithm, and a repeated power can generate a term xplogx. Such terms permit a wider family than ordinary integer-power polynomials, but their selection adds modeling uncertainty and requires validation.

Restricted cubic spline

Words: 44
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com

Geostatistics models spatial dependence for estimation and prediction. A mean or drift describes systematic variation, while a covariogram or semivariogram describes residual dependence. Kriging combines the two for spatial prediction.

Kriging

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Geostatistics OurBigBook.com
Kriging predicts an unobserved value of a spatial random field by combining observations according to their covariances. Nearest-neighbor interpolation uses the closest sample; kriging also asks how strongly each sample is related to the target and how much information the samples share with one another. Two nearby, highly correlated samples need not provide twice the information of one. The different forms of kriging depend on whether the mean is known, an unknown constant, or an unknown regression drift.
Write Z=(Z(s1​),…,Z(sn​))T for the observation random vector, z for its realized values, and Z0​=Z(s0​) for the prediction target. Assume finite second moments, and define
Σij​=Cov(Z(si​),Z(sj​)),ci​=Cov(Z(si​),Z0​),v0​=Var(Z0​).
(10)
Here Σ is the observation covariance matrix, assumed to be a positive-definite matrix in the formulas below. A covariance function supplies its entries and the target covariance vector c. For a second-order stationary random field, the covariogram C(h) depends on displacement, and the semivariogram satisfies γ(h)=C(0)−C(h). The intrinsically stationary random field formulation permits kriging using a semivariogram even when a stationary covariogram is unavailable; the finite covariance formulation below is a convenient important case.
For a linear combination wTZ predicting Z0​ with zero bias, the error variance equals its mean squared error:
Q(w)=E[(wTZ−Z0​)2]=v0​−2wTc+wTΣw.
(11)
Ordinary kriging and universal kriging minimize this quadratic form subject to their mean constraints. Their optimality is among the specified linear predictors with zero bias under the chosen statistical model; covariance information alone does not establish optimality among arbitrary nonlinear predictors. The Gaussian random field interpretation supplies additional conclusions in simple kriging.
The reported error variance assumes a chosen covariance function, its statistical parameters, observation locations, and a mean structure. It omits uncertainty in fitted covariance parameters and does not validate the trend. A repeated-sampling mean squared error need not equal the error variance conditional on each realized data vector.[ref]
In 1963, Georges Matheron presented kriging for estimating average ore grades in mining panels from weighted samples taken inside and outside a panel. This setting in geostatistics explains why prediction targets can be averages over regions as well as values at points.[ref]

Requiring wTZ to have zero bias for every β gives XTw=x0​. With known positive-definite matrix observation covariance matrix Σ, the minimizing weights solve

(13)

(14)
The first term is the estimated trend alone; the second predicts the correlated regression residuals. With q=x0​−XTΣ−1c, the error variance is

In the figure, the two colored curves are weighted probability density functions, with areas 1/3 and 2/3. Adding their heights at every x gives the black curve. Neither colored curve stops at a dividing line.

Every draw of W uses both random variables. Simultaneously applying a permutation to the mixture weights and mixture components leaves f unchanged. Thus identifiability of named components requires a convention, such as ordering distinct component means; label switching describes the associated inferential issue.[ref]
Even after choosing label names, identical mixture components reveal only their combined mixture weight, and an inactive mixture component has undetermined statistical parameters. Adding mixture components increases flexibility but can cause overfitting; judge predictions using cross-validation, rather than interpreting every fitted component as a discovered population.[ref]

Nonexchangeable weight priors can break exact symmetry but do not remove every multimodality problem.

Unbiased estimator OurBigBook.com
An unbiased estimator T is uniformly minimum-variance unbiased if its variance is no larger than that of every other unbiased estimator of the same parameter, for every parameter value. The Lehmann–Scheffé theorem gives such an estimator whenever an unbiased function of a complete sufficient statistic exists. Attaining the Cramér-Rao bound is sufficient for this property under its hypotheses, but is not necessary: for T∼Γ(n,λ) with n>2, (n−1)/T is unbiased and has variance λ2/(n−2), while the information bound is λ2/n. Completeness follows from uniqueness of the Laplace transform of h(t)tn−1, so the estimator is still uniformly optimal among unbiased estimators.

Deviance information criterion (DIC=D+pD​)

Words: 188 Articles: 2
Model selection OurBigBook.com
For Bayesian deviance D(θ)=−2logL(θ) under a common likelihood convention, define D=E[D(θ)∣y] and pD​=D−D(E[θ∣y]). Then DIC=D+pD​ trades average fit against effective complexity. Lower values suggest better penalized predictive fit in comparable models; differences are not Bayes factors or model posterior probabilities. The choice of stochastic parameters and latent-variable representation matters, especially in a hierarchical Bayesian model.

Effective parameter count in DIC (pD​=D−D(θ))

Words: 131 Articles: 1
Deviance information criterion OurBigBook.com
The DIC effective parameter count compares mean Bayesian deviance with deviance at the posterior mean. It need not be an integer or equal the number of coefficients. Interpretation depends on the parameterization and the chosen observational likelihood; nuisance intercepts count when they appear in that likelihood.
Quadratic posterior deviance moments (pD​=tr(JΣ))
Words: 89
Effective parameter count in DIC OurBigBook.com
Suppose the Bayesian deviance is locally D(θ)=D(θ)+(θ−θ)TJ(θ−θ) with positive-definite J, and the posterior is normal with mean m and covariance Σ. Writing b=m−θ, expectation and variance of the quadratic form give
E[D(θ)∣y]=D(θ)+bTJb+tr(JΣ),
(35)
Var[D(θ)∣y]=2tr{(JΣ)2}+4bTJΣJb.
(36)
Consequently the usual effective parameter count in DIC is pD​=tr(JΣ), whereas half the deviance variance is tr{(JΣ)2}+2bTJΣJb. A locally flat prior gives m=θ and Σ=J−1, so both counts equal the parameter dimension. Informative priors generally destroy their equality. The expectation formula requires only the first two moments; normality is used for the variance formula.

Variable selection

Words: 42
Model selection OurBigBook.com
Variable selection chooses which predictor variables enter a statistical model. The Lasso produces exact zero slopes along its Lasso regularization path; ridge regression generally shrinks without excluding variables. Selection for prediction should use predictive cross-validation or another stated criterion, rather than equating a coefficient p-value with practical usefulness.

Nonregular mixture model selection

Words: 65
Model selection OurBigBook.com
Testing the number of components in a finite mixture model is nonregular: absent components have zero weights on the parameter boundary and their means or other parameters are unidentified. The usual chi-squared limit for a likelihood-ratio test therefore need not apply. Information criteria are useful working comparisons, while parametric bootstrap and predictive cross-validation can provide more appropriate evidence. Neither a mixture fit nor a selected component count proves genuine latent populations.

Stepwise selection by the Akaike information criterion

Words: 160 Articles: 1
Akaike information criterion OurBigBook.com
Starting from a fitted model, compare admissible single-term additions and deletions within specified lower and upper scopes, retaining hierarchical lower-order terms when an interaction requires them. Select a change reducing the Akaike information criterion and repeat until no admissible change improves it. For a Gaussian normal linear model with N observations and k fitted mean coefficients, the criterion used by R's linear-model stepwise search is Nlog(RSS/N)+2k, up to constants common to the models. The search is greedy and need not find the best model in the whole scope. Ordinary coefficient tests in the selected model do not account for this model selection. The software arguments are documented in the MASS documentation.

Words: 54
Stepwise selection by the Akaike information criterion OurBigBook.com
Deleting q fitted mean parameters improves the Akaike information criterion exactly when the displayed condition holds, since the criterion difference is nlog(RSSreduced​/RSSfull​)−2q. For one parameter, the equivalent partial F-test statistic is below (n−p)(e2/n−1), where p is the full mean-model dimension. This is not the usual fixed-level significance-test cutoff. Fits must use the same observations and response transformation.

Pseudoreplication

Words: 82
Clustered data OurBigBook.com
Pseudoreplication treats dependent measurements from the same experimental unit as if they were independent treatment replicates. It exaggerates the effective sample size and commonly makes standard errors too small. In the pot example of replication in experimental design, counting twelve leaves per group as twelve independent treatment replicates ignores the four containing pots. The variance of nested measurements quantifies the resulting understatement of uncertainty. Nested measurements themselves are useful; pseudoreplication is the error of using them as independent replicates for the wrong level of inference.[ref]

Relative risk from group compositions (RR=p(1−a)a(1−p)​)

Words: 177 Articles: 1
Risk ratio OurBigBook.com
Let G be the event of membership in the first of two groups and A the event of selection. Write p=P(G), a=P(G∣A) and q=P(A)>0, with 0<p,a<1. Bayes' theorem gives the conditional probabilities r1​=P(A∣G)=aq/p and r0​=P(A∣Gc)=(1−a)q/(1−p). Their risk ratio is the displayed expression: the unknown overall selection probability cancels. Equivalently, it is the ratio of the group-membership odds after selection to those before selection.
When both selection probabilities lie strictly between zero and one, the selection odds ratio is [r1​/(1−r1​)]/[r0​/(1−r0​)] and generally depends on q. Thus compositions alone do not identify that odds ratio or provide sample sizes for a standard error. When a<p, the first group's observed selection rate is lower; this comparison alone does not establish a causal effect of group membership.

Relative risk bounds from rounded group compositions (pU​(1−aL​)aL​(1−pU​)​≤RR≤pL​(1−aU​)aU​(1−pL​)​)

Suppose 0<pL​≤p≤pU​<1 and 0<aL​≤a≤aU​<1. The formula for relative risk from group compositions increases with a and decreases with p, since a/(1−a) increases and (1−p)/p decreases. This monotonicity proves the displayed bounds. If percentages are rounded to the nearest whole percentage point, each corresponding proportion lies within 0.005 of its displayed value. These bounds describe rounding uncertainty; they are not a confidence interval for sampling uncertainty.

Log risk ratio (ℓ=log(p1​/p0​))

Words: 63
Risk ratio OurBigBook.com
The logarithm of a risk ratio is zero at equal risks, negative when the first risk is smaller, and positive when it is larger. For independent binomial event counts d1​,d0​ from samples n1​,n0​, its usual delta-method variance estimate is 1/d1​−1/n1​+1/d0​−1/n0​. This approximation requires nonzero counts; zero-event arms need another procedure. Log estimates are convenient for inverse-variance meta-analysis, and exponentiation returns to the risk-ratio scale.

Noncollapsibility of the odds ratio

Words: 91
Odds ratio OurBigBook.com
A conditional odds ratio can differ from the marginal odds ratio after averaging over a predictor, even without confounding. If conditional risks are pa​(x), averaging gives pˉ​a​=∫pa​(x)dF(x), and odds of pˉ​a​ are generally not averages of the conditional odds. Consequently a common conditional odds multiplier need not equal the marginal odds multiplier. However, if both groups use the same distribution F and p1​(x)>p0​(x) everywhere, then pˉ​1​>pˉ​0​ and the marginal odds ratio is still above one. Noncollapsibility alone cannot reverse a uniformly signed effect under an identical background distribution.

For two independent binomial groups with positive event and non-event counts (a,b) and (c,d), its estimate is log(ad/(bc)), with first-order variance 1/a+1/b+1/c+1/d by the delta method. Zero cells need a method that handles boundary data; the displayed normal approximation is not valid there.

Log odds ratio OurBigBook.com
For two independent binomial distributions with event and nonevent counts a,b and c,d, the odds ratio is ad/(bc). The delta method applied to log(p/(1−p)), whose derivative is 1/[p(1−p)], gives a group variance 1/[Np(1−p)]. Substitution of the fitted proportion gives 1/a+1/b in the first group and 1/c+1/d in the second. Their independence gives the displayed sum. A normal approximation then gives a confidence interval on the log odds ratio scale; exponentiation produces an odds-ratio interval. Zero cells require another approximation or model.

Bootstrapping (statistics)

Words: 1k Articles: 16
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
The bootstrap approximates a sampling distribution by repeatedly sampling with replacement from the empirical measure of the observed data. In the ordinary nonparametric version, observations are assumed independent and identically distributed; a bootstrap sample has the same size as the original statistical sample. A statistic, such as a sample mean or sample median, is recomputed on each resample. Its variation across resamples estimates how the original statistic would vary across repeated sampling from the unknown probability distribution.[ref]
The key distinction is between the observed statistical sample and its still-unknown source probability distribution. Condition on the observed values x1​,…,xn​ and form the empirical measure
Pn​=n1​∑i=1n​δxi​​.
(51)
Here δxi​​ is a Dirac measure. Draw independent indices I1​,…,In​ from the uniform distribution on a finite set {1,…,n} and set Xj∗​=xIj​​. Each observed slot has probability 1/n on every draw. If equal values occupy several slots, their total probability is the sum of those slot probabilities; distinct observed values need not be equally likely. A star denotes this conditional resampling experiment. There are nn equally likely ordered index sequences, although bootstrap count vectors and statistics can combine many such sequences.
A complicated sampling distribution need not stop statistical inference when recomputing the statistic is easy. The bootstrap reuses that calculation on simulated datasets. The plug-in estimator principle replaces the unknown probability measure by Pn​ in the whole repeated-sampling experiment. Whether that substitution approximates the target sampling distribution needs an appropriate bootstrap consistency theorem for the sample mean or a result for the particular statistic. A larger number of resamples reduces Monte Carlo error; it cannot repair the bootstrap failure for a uniform endpoint, an unrepresentative statistical sample or ignored statistical dependence.[ref]

Exact bootstrap distribution for three observations (P∗​(X∗=7/3)=2/9)

Words: 231
Bootstrapping (statistics) OurBigBook.com
Take the original observations (1,2,4), with sample mean x=7/3. All 33=27 ordered bootstrap samples have probability 1/27. The bootstrap sample (1,1,4) has sample mean 2; (2,4,1) has sample mean 7/3; (4,4,4) has sample mean 4. These are illustrative possibilities, not three simulated measurements used to estimate the distribution.
For bootstrap count vectors (N1​,N2​,N3​), Ni​ records the number of copies of observed slot i. Their multinomial distribution is
P∗​((N1​,N2​,N3​)=(a,b,c))=a!b!c!3!​271​,a+b+c=3,
(52)
and X∗=(N1​+2N2​+4N3​)/3. Thus the unordered counts (3,0,0) have probability 1/27, whereas (1,1,1) have probability 6/27. Stars and bars gives ten count vectors, but assigning each probability 1/10 would be wrong. Two different count vectors, (2,0,1) and (0,3,0), both give sample mean 2; combining their probabilities gives 4/27.
The conditional bootstrap variance of a sample mean gives a compact check on the enumeration. Each resampled draw has expected value 7/3 and variance
31​[(1−37​)2+(2−37​)2+(4−37​)2]=914​.
(53)
Averaging three independent draws divides that variance by three:
E∗​[X∗]=37​,Var∗​(X∗)=2714​.​
(54)
The exact conditional bootstrap standard error is 14/27​≃0.720. The original sample variance with denominator n−1 is 7/3, so its usual estimated standard error for the sample mean is 7/9​≃0.882. Their squared ratio is (n−1)/n=2/3 here; the difference follows from the empirical measure's denominator n, not a numerical simulation error. Neither number is the known true sampling standard error of the unknown source probability distribution.

Bootstrap failure for a uniform endpoint (P∗​(X(n)∗​=X(n)​)=1−(1−1/n)n)

Words: 68
Bootstrapping (statistics) OurBigBook.com
For a continuous uniform distribution on [0,θ], the scaled maximum gap n(θ−X(n)​)/θ tends to a unit-rate exponential distribution. An ordinary bootstrap sample includes the unique observed maximum with probability 1−(1−1/n)n→1−e−1. The bootstrap maximum gap therefore retains an atom at zero, whereas the target limit is continuous. This proves failure of the ordinary empirical bootstrap for this endpoint functional; consistency of the endpoint estimate alone does not justify resampling its extreme-value limit.

Replace the unknown sampling distribution by the empirical distribution, generate independent bootstrap samples, and recompute the statistic. The sample standard deviation of those recomputed values estimates the conditional bootstrap standard deviation, which approximates the statistic's sampling standard error when the bootstrap is consistent. It is different from the Monte Carlo standard error of the estimated bootstrap mean.

A bootstrap confidence interval uses the conditional resampling distribution of an estimator to choose its endpoints. Basic intervals invert bootstrap error quantiles; percentile intervals use quantiles of the resampled estimates themselves. Their asymptotic coverage requires conditions appropriate to the statistic and interval construction.

Bootstrap confidence interval OurBigBook.com
For θ=β1​β2​, use θ=β​1​β​2​. Under regular regression assumptions, the delta method gives standard error s=(d⊤Vd)1/2, where d=(β​2​,β​1​)⊤ and V estimates the covariance of the regression estimate. Resample the observational units, refit, and compute both θ∗ and s∗. A percentile bootstrap confidence interval uses the .025 and .975 quantiles of θ∗. A bootstrap-t confidence interval uses quantiles of (θ∗−θ)/s∗ and reverses them when solving for θ. If both true coefficients vanish, the first derivative is zero and the standard first-order justification is unavailable; product-specific nonregular inference is then needed.

If qp​ are conditional quantiles of T∗ and s is the original estimated standard error, invert the studentized inequalities to obtain the displayed interval. The quantile order is reversed by subtraction. Its coverage is approximate and requires a nondegenerate statistic and suitable bootstrap regularity.

With B simulated estimates, ranks near (B+1)α/2 and (B+1)(1−α/2) provide an approximate central 1−α confidence interval. Unlike a basic bootstrap confidence interval, the endpoints are not reflected about the observed estimate. Coverage requires suitable regularity and accurate bootstrap approximation; the ranks do not establish exact finite-sample coverage.

Bootstrap sample

Words: 313 Articles: 4
Bootstrapping (statistics) OurBigBook.com
A bootstrap sample of size n is drawn by sampling with replacement from the n observed data slots. Some observations occur repeatedly. For a given slot, every draw misses it with probability 1−1/n, so its omission probability after n independent draws is
P∗​(Ni​=0)=(1−n1​)n⟶e−1.
(55)
By linearity of expectation, the expected number of omitted slots is n(1−1/n)n, whether or not their omission events are independent. For the three-observation exact bootstrap distribution for three observations, an individual slot is omitted with probability 8/27 and the expected number of omitted slots is 8/9. This finite-sample calculation explains both repeated values and incomplete coverage; e−1 is a limiting expected proportion, not an exact fraction in every resample.

For independent mean-zero errors in a fixed-design regression, form yi∗​=xi⊤​β​+ei​Wi​, where the independent multipliers have mean zero and variance one, and refit. Rademacher multipliers taking the values −1 and 1 with equal probability are a simple choice. Conditional on the data, the bootstrap errors have mean zero and preserve observation-specific residual variances, supporting heteroscedasticity rather than imposing a common residual distribution. Appropriate leverage corrections and regularity assumptions are required for accurate studentized inference.

This preserves the empirical within-pair dependence needed to estimate a correlation coefficient or another joint statistic. Independently resampling the two margins destroys that dependence and estimates a different sampling law.

Asymptotic mean squared error (AMSE)

Mean squared error OurBigBook.com
The asymptotic mean squared error is the leading large-sample approximation to the sum of variance and squared bias of an estimator. Minimizing it balances stochastic variation against systematic error; the resulting choice must still satisfy the assumptions used in the approximation.

If independent observations have mean θ and variance θ2, the scaled sample mean has
MSE(kXˉ)=θ2[(k−1)2+k2/n].
(58)
For θ=0, it improves on the unbiased sample mean precisely when (n−1)/(n+1)<k<1. The optimal scale is k=n/(n+1) and its risk is θ2/(n+1). At θ=0 all risks vanish and strict improvement is impossible.

Under the usual smoothness and shrinking-bandwidth assumptions, the leading mean integrated squared error is the displayed sum of integrated variance and squared bias of an estimator. Its minimizer is h=[R(K)/(nμ2​(K)2R(f′′))]1/5, giving order n−4/5. An added O(n−1) integrated covariance term is lower order at this bandwidth and does not change its leading constant.

Risk function OurBigBook.com
A decision rule is admissible if no other rule has risk function no greater at every parameter and strictly smaller at one parameter. Parameter estimation is one decision problem; its admissible rules are admissible estimators.

An estimator is admissible when no other estimator has risk no larger at every parameter value and strictly smaller at at least one value.

James–Stein shrinkage toward the sample mean (θ=Xˉ1p​+(1−(p−3)/∥X−Xˉ1p​∥2)(X−Xˉ1p​))
Words: 70
James–Stein estimator OurBigBook.com
For X∼Np​(θ,I) and p≥4, this estimator preserves the sample mean and applies James–Stein shrinkage in its orthogonal (p−1)-dimensional contrast subspace. Its risk under quadratic loss is p−(p−3)2Eθ​∥X−Xˉ1p​∥−2. The noncentrality is ∥θ−θˉ1p​∥2, so the reciprocal moment of a noncentral chi-squared variable makes the risk minimal exactly when all true components coincide; the minimum is 3. A negative realized shrinkage factor reverses contrast signs, and its magnitude can exceed one for sufficiently small contrast norm.

The James-Stein risk is strictly below the dimension at every finite parameter, but its improvement tends to zero as the mean norm tends to infinity. Strict pointwise domination therefore leaves the supremum risk unchanged.

Minimax risk (R∗)

Words: 88 Articles: 1
Minimax estimator OurBigBook.com
The minimax risk is the infimum over estimators of the supremum of their risk functions over a parameter class. An upper bound supplies an estimator; a lower bound applies to every estimator, often using the Le Cam two-point lemma.
Pointwise versus uniform risk distinction (supm​Rn​(m))
Words: 56
Minimax risk OurBigBook.com
A risk function can decay rapidly for each fixed regression function while its supremum over a function class decays more slowly or fails to decay. Bounds depending on each function's local differentiability remainder need not be uniform. In fixed-design nonparametric regression, a class with no common smoothness bound permits smooth bump functions whose supports shrink between design points. Such sequences obstruct uniform estimation without contradicting fixed-function mean squared error bounds.

Orthogonal statistical parameters (Iψη​=E(uψ​uη​)=0)

Words: 480 Articles: 7
Fisher information matrix OurBigBook.com
Two statistical parameters are orthogonal when their cross term in the expected Fisher information matrix vanishes. This is pointwise orthogonality at a specified parameter value, or global orthogonality when it holds throughout the parameter domain. It gives a zero cross covariance in the regular first-order asymptotic distribution of efficient estimators, rather than asserting exact finite-sample independence.
Score factorization implies parameter orthogonality (ℓψ​=λtψ​⟹Iψλ​=0)
Words: 61
Orthogonal statistical parameters OurBigBook.com
In a regular common-support statistical model with probability density function a(λ,y)eλt(y;ψ), the score function in ψ is λtψ​. Its zero expectation gives Etψ​=0 for λ=0. The mixed log-likelihood derivative is tψ​, so the cross Fisher information matrix block vanishes. At zero the same conclusion follows by continuity when the regular derivatives extend there. This proves parameter orthogonality; it does not establish exact independence of fitted parameters.
Orthogonal coefficient blocks in a centered normal linear model (X1T​X2​=0)
Words: 63
Orthogonal statistical parameters OurBigBook.com
In a normal linear model whose predictor columns are orthogonal to the intercept, two coefficient blocks are orthogonal statistical parameters precisely when the cross-block Fisher information is zero, equivalently the displayed design cross-product vanishes. Then XTX is block diagonal, so the corresponding least-squares estimators have zero covariance and, being jointly Gaussian, are independent. Their fitted subspaces are orthogonal and their extra sums of squares do not depend on which block is added first.
Cox-Reid adjusted profile likelihood (ℓCR​(ψ)=ℓp​(ψ)−21​log∣jλλ​(ψ,λψ​)∣)
Words: 76
Orthogonal statistical parameters OurBigBook.com
For a regular interest/nuisance parameterization with parameter orthogonality, this nuisance-information adjustment approximates a conditional likelihood construction and reduces first-order nuisance effects. It is related to modified profile likelihood but is not a universal substitute for its sample-coordinate Jacobian. When the constrained and full nuisance fits coincide in the relevant ancillary coordinates, that Jacobian is one and the two expressions agree. For normal variance with unknown mean, it replaces the profile's n by the residual n−1 in the logarithmic variance term.
Local orthogonal nuisance reparametrization (∂ψ​λ(ψ,η)=−Iλλ−1​Iλψ​)
Words: 71
Orthogonal statistical parameters OurBigBook.com
For scalar interest parameter ψ, choose new nuisance coordinates η and keep ψ fixed. The transformed interest score function is Uψ​+Uλ⊤​∂ψ​λ, so the displayed differential equation makes its Fisher information cross-block with the nuisance score zero. Under smoothness and nonsingularity it has a local solution from initial coordinates on a fixed interest slice. Orthogonality is local expected-information decoupling; it implies first-order asymptotic independence of fitted blocks, not exact independence or nuisance-free conditional inference.
Negative binomial mean-size parameter orthogonality (Iμθ​=0)
Words: 47
Orthogonal statistical parameters OurBigBook.com
For the negative binomial distribution with mean μ>0 and size θ>0, the one-observation score function in the mean is uμ​=θ(y−μ)/[μ(μ+θ)]. Its size derivative is (y−μ)/(μ+θ)2, whose expectation is zero. Thus the expected Fisher information matrix is diagonal in (μ,θ). Regular interior maximum-likelihood estimators have zero asymptotic cross covariance, without necessarily being independent in finite samples.
Interest-respecting reparametrization
Words: 111 Articles: 1
Orthogonal statistical parameters OurBigBook.com
An interest-respecting reparametrization preserves the parameter of interest, or changes it only by a one-to-one function of itself. The nuisance parameter may depend on both old parameters, provided the complete transformation is smoothly invertible. Thus the level sets representing the inferential target are unchanged. Orthogonality can be sought by choosing the new nuisance coordinate along solutions of the orthogonalization equation for two statistical parameters.
Orthogonalization equation for two statistical parameters (∂ψ∂λ​​η​=−Iλλ​Iψλ​​)
Words: 54
Interest-respecting reparametrization OurBigBook.com
Write the old nuisance parameter as λ=g(ψ,η) with gη​=0. The transformed score functions are uψnew​=uψ​+gψ​uλ​ and uη​=gη​uλ​. Their expected cross product is gη​(Iψλ​+gψ​Iλλ​). Setting it to zero gives the displayed ordinary differential equation along fixed-η curves, assuming positive nuisance Fisher information. Smooth solutions with distinct initial conditions give a local interest-respecting orthogonal coordinate system.

Jeffreys prior (πJ​(θ)∝detI(θ)​)

Words: 262 Articles: 3
Fisher information matrix OurBigBook.com
The Jeffreys prior uses the square root of the determinant of the Fisher information matrix as a parameter-density kernel. It is invariant under smooth one-to-one reparameterization, since the information and density Jacobians transform compatibly. It may be an improper prior; invariance does not guarantee posterior propriety. With nuisance parameters, a scalar conditional Jeffreys prior and the joint Jeffreys prior need not coincide.
Proper gamma approximation to a Poisson Jeffreys prior (Gamma(1/2,ε),ε↓0)
Words: 62
Jeffreys prior OurBigBook.com
A Poisson distribution with mean Eλ and positive known exposure has Fisher information E/λ, so its Jeffreys prior kernel is λ−1/2. The proper shape-rate gamma distribution Gamma(1/2,ε) has kernel λ−1/2e−ελ, approximating the improper kernel where ελ is small. Its posterior is Gamma(y+1/2,E+ε), converging to Gamma(y+1/2,E). There is no normalized Jeffreys prior to which the proper priors converge weakly; this is kernel approximation and posterior convergence.
Jeffreys prior for a scale parameter (πJ​(σ)∝1/σ)
Words: 34
Jeffreys prior OurBigBook.com
For a differentiable scale family with finite positive Fisher information, the score is −[1+u(logf)′(u)]/σ. Its squared expectation is a constant times σ−2, yielding the displayed Jeffreys prior. This is an improper prior on the entire positive half-line.
Jeffreys prior for an additive variance component (π(v)∝21​∑s​(v+rs​)−2​)
Words: 109
Jeffreys prior OurBigBook.com
For independent normal observations with fixed means and variances v+rs​, where v≥0 is unknown and all known rs​>0, the scalar Fisher information for v is Ivv​=21​∑s​(v+rs​)−2. Thus its scalar Jeffreys prior is finite at zero and behaves like 1/v at infinity. Unlike a log-flat prior 1/v, it avoids a divergent integral at the zero-variance boundary. After flat-prior elimination of a Gaussian common mean, the integrated likelihood is bounded by a constant times v−(N−1)/2, so this prior yields a proper posterior for N>1 and a proper prior on any remaining mean-shape parameters. In the homoscedastic case it reduces to 1/(v+r), which is log-flat for the total variance rather than for the latent variance alone.
